arguments.name: John Cook's thesis: Paul taught bodily resurrection
arguments.conclusion: Paul's view of the resurrection is that he saw the same bodily appearances of Jesus described in the Gospels (Matthew, Luke, John), not a ghostly or non-bodily view.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas (reporting John Cook)
premises: Cook states his thesis up front in his resurrection volume, published in the respected German Wissenschaftliche series.
Cook explicitly denies that Paul teaches a 'Casper' (ghostly) view of resurrection appearances.
Cook holds that Paul teaches the same bodily appearances found in Matthew, Luke, and John.

st1.quote: my thesis is that Paul's view of the resurrection is that he saw the same body as described in the Gospels

st2.quote: He says, "Before you read, I'm going to give you my thesis statement up front."

st3.quote: they're both included in the uh German uh Wissenschaftliche series, which is now hundreds of volumes

st4.quote: He teaches the same bodily appearances Matthew, Luke, and John do.

st6.quote: He means not this wispy Mike Mike wrote a some treatments of this and he says um Mike called those views like I call them Jedi Jesus.

arguments.prior_art: John Cook, 'Empty Tomb' volumes on crucifixion and resurrection (Wissenschaftliche series)

or1.quote: He's doing mostly Greco- Greco-Roman historiography.
or1.why: Cook's historiographical method applied to Paul's resurrection view is not a restatement of prior apologetic arguments.

or2.quote: they're both included in the uh German uh Wissenschaftliche series, which is now hundreds of volumes
or2.why: Cites publication venue and Cook's Greco-Roman historiographical method as support.

or3.quote: He's doing mostly Greco- Greco-Roman historiography.
or3.why: Connects Greco-Roman historiography to NT resurrection studies.

arguments.weakest_link: The premise that Cook's thesis accurately represents Paul's view rests only on Cook's assertion, not on exegesis of the texts.
arguments.develop_next: Provide the actual Pauline texts Cook cites (e.g., 1 Cor 15) to show the bodily reading is exegetically forced.

arguments.name: Bodily resurrection view is now widely accepted
arguments.conclusion: The view that Paul believed in bodily resurrection is now very widely taught, despite being extremely unpopular when Cook's books first appeared.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: Cook's bodily-resurrection thesis was extremely unpopular when his volumes first came out.
The fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is now very widely taught by scholars today.

st1.quote: now it's kind of taken the day, the fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is very widely taught today

st2.quote: That's extremely impo- unpopular when this these books first came out or even after.

st4.quote: Very widely taught by the guys.

st6.quote: now it's kind of taken the day, the fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is very widely taught today

st8.quote: Very widely taught by the guys.

arguments.prior_art: N.T. Wright, 'The Resurrection of the Son of God', 2003

or1.quote: now it's kind of taken the day, the fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is very widely taught today
or1.why: A variant of the standard scholarly-consensus claim, updated to the post-Cook era.

or2.quote: That's extremely impo- unpopular when this these books first came out or even after.
or2.why: Adds the historical reception data about Cook's unpopularity.

arguments.weakest_link: The consensus claim is asserted without naming or counting the scholars who hold it.
arguments.develop_next: Give a concrete list or survey of scholars now teaching the bodily view to substantiate 'very widely taught'.

arguments.name: Dale Allison concedes Paul meant bodily resurrection
arguments.conclusion: Even a scholar not personally committed to the bodily view, Dale Allison, affirms that Paul meant bodily resurrection.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas (reporting Dale Allison)
premises: Dale Allison says Paul believed in bodily resurrection appearances like the Gospels do.
Allison states he is more open to non-bodily things and is not on the bodily side himself.
Allison insists one must distinguish what Paul said from what Bultmann said about Paul.

st1.quote: Dale Allison said Paul believed in bodily resurrection appearance like the Gospels do.

st2.quote: Dale says, "I'm more open to non-bodily things but I am telling you even though I'm not on that interpret- I'm not in the bodily side in my view, I think Paul meant bodily resurrection.

st3.quote: You have got to make this distinguish between what Paul said and somebody else going "Well, Bultmann says Paul believed bodily resurrection."

st4.quote: I think Paul meant bodily resurrection.

st6.quote: I'm more open to non-bodily things but I am telling you even though I'm not on that interpret- I'm not in the bodily side in my view, I think Paul meant bodily resurrection.

st8.quote: Dale Allison said Paul believed in bodily resurrection appearance like the Gospels do.

or1.quote: Dale Allison said Paul believed in bodily resurrection appearance like the Gospels do.
or1.why: A variant of the standard critical-concession argument, citing a specific non-committed scholar.

or2.quote: I'm more open to non-bodily things but I am telling you even though I'm not on that interpret- I'm not in the bodily side in my view, I think Paul meant bodily resurrection.
or2.why: Uses Allison's self-described non-commitment as evidence, which prior art does not foreground.

arguments.weakest_link: The claim that Allison is 'not on the bodily side' is asserted by Habermas, not demonstrated from Allison's own texts.
arguments.develop_next: Quote Allison's own methodological caveats verbatim to show he is a genuinely hostile witness.

arguments.name: Bultmann affirmed Paul taught bodily resurrection
arguments.conclusion: Bultmann himself acknowledged that Paul believed in bodily resurrection, even though Bultmann did not accept it.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: Bultmann can say Paul believed in bodily resurrection while personally rejecting it.
This is the distinction Allison was drawing between Paul's view and Bultmann's own view.

st1.quote: But Bultmann can say Paul believed it, but I don't.

st2.quote: You have got to make this distinguish between what Paul said and somebody else going "Well, Bultmann says Paul believed bodily resurrection."

st4.quote: But Bultmann can say Paul believed it, but I don't.

st6.quote: But Bultmann can say Paul believed it, but I don't.

arguments.prior_art: Rudolf Bultmann, 'Theology of the New Testament', 1948-1953

or1.quote: But Bultmann can say Paul believed it, but I don't.
or1.why: A variant of the standard 'even Bultmann conceded' move.

arguments.weakest_link: No citation to any Bultmann text is given; the concession is asserted from memory.
arguments.develop_next: Cite the exact Bultmann passage where he grants Paul's bodily view.

arguments.name: Cook's narrow view is credible, not fundamentalist
arguments.conclusion: John Cook's adoption of a narrow bodily-resurrection view is a stunning and credible scholarly move, not the product of fundamentalist bias.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: Cook states up front that he is taking a narrow view.
Cook would not be blamed as one of the 'fighting fundy' type guys.
German scholarship still carries a certain credibility of scholarship.

st2.quote: you wouldn't blame him with being one of these fighting fundy type guys at all

st3.quote: German scholarship still means German scholarship.

st4.quote: you wouldn't blame him with being one of these fighting fundy type guys at all

st6.quote: you wouldn't blame him with being one of these fighting fundy type guys at all

st8.quote: German scholarship still means German scholarship.

arguments.prior_art: John Cook, Wissenschaftliche-series volumes on crucifixion and resurrection

or1.quote: you wouldn't blame him with being one of these fighting fundy type guys at all
or1.why: A variant of the 'hostile witness' credibility move, applied to Cook specifically.

or2.quote: German scholarship still means German scholarship.

arguments.weakest_link: The inference from 'not a fundy' to 'credible scholarship' is a reputation appeal, not evidence.
arguments.develop_next: Show Cook's method is critical by citing his non-confessional handling of Greco-Roman sources.

arguments.name: Wright compares resurrection knowability to Caesar's Rubicon
arguments.conclusion: The resurrection is as historically knowable as Julius Caesar crossing the Rubicon.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas (reporting Tom Wright)
premises: Tom Wright made a comment comparing the knowability of the resurrection to Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon.
Habermas and his interlocutor recognize the quote and attribute it to Wright.

st1.quote: the resurrection is as knowable as the Rubicon

st2.quote: There's it's as solid to me as the Jesus raised from the dead as a Julius Caesar crossed the uh Is that Pardon me?

st4.quote: the resurrection is as knowable as the Rubicon

st6.quote: Now, because I don't buy it, it didn't stun me as being super positive

arguments.prior_art: N.T. Wright, 'The Resurrection of the Son of God', 2003

or1.quote: the resurrection is as knowable as the Rubicon
or1.why: A variant of Wright's historical-knowability claim, compressed into an analogy.

or3.quote: the resurrection is as knowable as the Rubicon
or3.why: Connects Roman political history to resurrection historiography.

arguments.weakest_link: The analogy is reported second-hand and never unpacked; no criterion of knowability is given.
arguments.develop_next: State the historical criteria under which the Rubicon and the resurrection are equally knowable.
